There's a very ancient lineage of stories about a non-human female group that goes to bathe in water, and a human male tricks them by stealing their clothes on the bank. In some stories, this prevents them from shapechanging back into their alien creature forms - in others, it's just their modesty that keeps them in the water. Eventually the male human gives back the clothes (or in some myths, discarded skins of human appearance) and all but one of the female alien creatures leaves - the remaining one becomes the wife of the human.

In many versions of the story, the union is not a happy one and the female alien either tries to get away from her captor, or she is unwillingly separated from him.

This also crosses many cultures, too. See Volundarkvida in the Nordic tales for a smith who trapped a birdlike maiden (she disappears and leaves him, never to return, although the start of the tale implies he expects her to eventually). Also see the tale of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl for a similar treatment in Chinese fables - although the weaver girl is associated with magpies, and on the 7th day of the 7th month the two can be reunited by a bridge of birds.

I did some digging into the antagonist, since he's historically pretty important to the setting's politics and I wanted to make him a more fleshed-out darklord.

What I found was a bit surprising. In the second edition, he hailed from a distant region, which is on the "other side of the world" from the main campaign tales (on a separate continent). In that region, a corrupt bishop had seized power in a midnight coup involving mobilization of masses of undead soldiers. The antagonist could quite feasibly have heard of this.

The bishop also had a human warlord serving him.

I changed the antagonist's backstory so that he knew of this, and that was his "moral line in the sand" - although he himself was bloodthirsty and cruel, he would absolutely not tolerate necromancy and commanding the undead. He swore to fight the bishop and the warlord.

The antagonist was pulled into the demiplane, and believed himself to be fighting the bishop's forces when he arrived in his primary domain (perhaps understandably, since the domain is no stranger to wandering undead). The lich lord took personal note of the antagonist's arrival and held a direct audience with him, eventually misdirecting him southwards to a neighboring domain.

Coincidentally, that neighboring domain was ruled by... a Count! The antagonist and his men launched several successful raids against the locals before they became aware of the lich lord's duplicity. Overmatched by the eventual organized local response, they fled into the mists and back into his primary domain a second time, facing the lich lord as he openly led his undead border guards to repel them. Defeated and near capture, the antagonist and his men crossed one final time into a newly-formed domain.

The antagonist eventually pieced together parts of the truth: he believes the lich lord may be the same person as the bishop, or possibly not. But he is 100% certain that the lich lord is an undead horror and is the secret source and commander of the undead hordes that the entire region rightly fears.

He has tried to unite the other human-ruled domains against the lich lord to overthrow this monstrous ruler, but his overtures have been ignored or subverted by the others. He has led various campaigns against them to overthrow their indifferent leadership and install friendly regimes who will unite to oust the lich lord.

The real tragedy of the antagonist's plight is that he is actually entirely correct, but he knows (Cassandra-like) that his shouted truths fall upon deaf ears. The other human rulers are content to continue doing trade with the primary domain and feeding into the lich lord's coffers, all while the inscrutable lich lord continues to pursue his sinister goals with the resources of the region's largest nation under his command.
